# A Field-Theoretic Approach to Gravitational Energy and Cosmology

## Deriving the Gravitational Energy-Momentum Tensor

The gravitational energy-momentum tensor can be derived directly from the Einstein equations by adopting a field-theoretic approach formulated in Minkowski space. Rather than treating gravity purely as the geometry of curved spacetime, this method reinterprets the gravitational field as a physical field propagating against a flat background. Within this framework, the Einstein equations can be recast so that they are expressed as an acceleration tensor that is proportional to the total energy-momentum tensor. This reformulation clarifies the physical status of gravitational energy, placing it on an equal footing with the energy and momentum of matter and other fields, and providing a well-defined tensorial quantity that governs gravitational dynamics.

## The Cancellation of Energy in Flat-Space Cosmology

A striking consequence of this approach emerges in the context of flat-space cosmology. Here, the gravitational energy carries a negative sign, and its magnitude is precisely such that it exactly cancels the positive energy contributed by matter. The net result is a universe in which the total energy vanishes identically. This exact cancellation is not accidental but follows naturally from the structure of the theory, and it lends support to the notion that the cosmos as a whole may possess zero total energy—a feature with profound implications for our understanding of cosmic origins.

## Bimetric Coupling and Coordinate Invariance

The relativistic theory of gravitation underlying this construction employs a bimetric coupling between two distinct metrics: the dynamical Riemann metric, which describes the curved geometry experienced by matter, and the fixed Minkowski metric, which provides the flat background reference. The interplay between these two metrics is central to the theory's formulation. However, this coupling comes at a conceptual cost: the presence of a preferred flat background metric breaks the general coordinate invariance that is a hallmark of standard general relativity. While this represents a departure from the full diffeomorphism symmetry of Einstein's theory, it is precisely this feature that enables the consistent definition of gravitational energy and momentum as genuine tensorial quantities.

## A Singularity-Free Black Hole Solution

One of the notable achievements of this framework is the analytic solution of a singularity-free version of the Schwarzschild black hole. In the conventional Schwarzschild solution, the interior region is plagued by a central singularity, and the metric components associated with time and radial directions exchange their roles across the event horizon. In the present formulation, by contrast, the interior metric components smoothly die out without ever changing sign. As a consequence, the usual physical role of time is preserved throughout the interior, and the pathological singularity is entirely avoided. This yields a physically well-behaved description of gravitational collapse and black hole interiors.

## Cosmological Implications: ΛCDM and Early-Time Inflation

Finally, the cosmological model built upon this theory successfully reproduces the well-established ΛCDM framework, thereby remaining consistent with the wealth of observational data that supports the standard model of cosmology. Beyond this agreement, the model naturally generates a form of early-time inflation. Remarkably, during this inflationary epoch both the total energy and the zero-point energy vanish. This provides an elegant mechanism for the accelerated expansion of the early universe while simultaneously maintaining the vanishing total energy that characterizes the theory. In this way, the framework unifies a description of inflationary cosmology with the deep principle of zero total cosmic energy, offering a coherent picture that spans from the earliest moments of the universe to its large-scale structure today.

# A Field-Theoretic Approach to Gravitation: Black Holes and Cosmology in the Relativistic Theory of Gravitation

## Introduction and Theoretical Framework

This work develops a field-theoretic treatment of gravitation formulated within the fixed background of Minkowski space, in contrast to the geometric interpretation of general relativity where spacetime curvature is the fundamental object. Central to this approach is the derivation of the gravitational energy-momentum tensor directly from the Einstein equations. By treating the gravitational field as a physical field propagating on a flat spacetime background, one obtains a well-defined, localizable energy-momentum tensor for gravity itself—an object that is notoriously ambiguous in the purely geometric formulation, where it appears only as a pseudo-tensor.

The particular framework employed here is the relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG). A defining feature of this theory is the introduction of a bimetric structure: alongside the dynamical Riemannian metric that describes the gravitational field, the flat Minkowski metric is retained as a genuine physical entity. The coupling between these two metrics—characterized by a massive graviton term proportional to the cosmological constant—explicitly breaks the general coordinate invariance that underlies standard general relativity. This breaking of symmetry has profound consequences, replacing the gauge freedom of Einstein's theory with additional physical constraints and modifying the structure of solutions in strong-field regimes.

## Application to Black Holes

When this formalism is applied to the problem of a spherically symmetric mass, the results differ markedly from those of the classical Schwarzschild solution. The bimetric constraints, together with the presence of the massive graviton term, regularize the geometry so that the black hole solution obtained is entirely free of the central singularity that plagues the standard general-relativistic description. The pathological point of infinite curvature at the origin is eliminated.

Remarkably, the resulting Schwarzschild-type black hole is analytically solvable, allowing the physical properties of the object—its horizon structure, causal boundaries, and field distribution—to be examined in closed form. The absence of a singularity, combined with analytic tractability, provides a compelling and internally consistent picture of gravitational collapse that avoids the conceptual difficulties associated with infinite densities and undefined physical quantities.

## Cosmological Consequences

Extending the theory to cosmological scales, the analysis incorporates a positive cosmological constant and successfully reproduces the observationally favored ΛCDM model. This is the standard model of modern cosmology, describing a universe dominated at late times by dark energy (the cosmological constant Λ) and cold dark matter (CDM), and consistent with a broad array of observations from the cosmic microwave background to large-scale structure.

Beyond recovering the established late-time behavior, the field-theoretic framework naturally accommodates a phase of early-time inflation. The rapid accelerated expansion of the primordial universe emerges from the dynamics of the theory, addressing the horizon and flatness problems and providing the initial conditions from which structure subsequently forms. Thus, the single framework spans the cosmic history from the inflationary epoch through to the present dark-energy-dominated era.

## Energy Balance and Zero-Point Energy

Perhaps the most significant result of this investigation concerns the global energy budget of the universe. Within this formulation, the total energy of the system is found to vanish identically. This cancellation arises because the gravitational energy—captured precisely by the derived energy-momentum tensor—exactly balances the energy contained in matter and radiation. The negative gravitational energy compensates the positive material energy, yielding a net total of zero.

Equally important, the zero-point energy is shown to vanish within this scheme. This addresses one of the deepest problems in theoretical physics: the enormous discrepancy between the vacuum energy predicted by quantum field theory and the tiny value inferred from cosmological observations. The vanishing of both the total energy and the zero-point energy, together with the exact cancellation between gravitational and material contributions, lends strong internal consistency to the field-theoretic and relativistic theory of gravitation approach and offers a natural resolution to longstanding puzzles regarding the energy content of the universe.

## Conclusion

By grounding gravitation in a Minkowski-space field theory and deriving the gravitational energy-momentum tensor from the Einstein equations, this work demonstrates that the relativistic theory of gravitation—with its symmetry-breaking bimetric coupling—yields physically appealing results across vastly different scales. It produces a singularity-free, analytically solvable black hole, reproduces the ΛCDM cosmology complete with an early inflationary phase, and, most significantly, establishes that the total energy and zero-point energy of the universe both vanish through the exact cancellation of gravitational and material energy.

# Minkowski and Einstein: Reshaping Our Understanding of Space and Time

## Starting Point: A Revolution in Physics

The story of modern physics begins with a profound shift in how we understand the universe. At the heart of this transformation lie two remarkable figures whose ideas became deeply intertwined: Albert Einstein and Hermann Minkowski.

## Einstein's Bold Beginning

In 1905, Albert Einstein published his special theory of relativity, fundamentally challenging the classical Newtonian view of the cosmos. Starting from two simple postulates—that the laws of physics are the same for all observers in uniform motion, and that the speed of light remains constant regardless of the observer's motion—Einstein arrived at revolutionary conclusions. Time could slow down, lengths could contract, and mass and energy proved to be interchangeable, captured in the iconic equation E=mc².

## Minkowski's Elegant Framework

Interestingly, Hermann Minkowski had once been Einstein's mathematics professor. Initially skeptical of his former student's abilities, Minkowski later became one of the most important interpreters of relativity. In 1908, he introduced a groundbreaking mathematical framework that unified space and time into a single four-dimensional continuum, now famously known as "spacetime."

Minkowski declared:

> "Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality."

## A Lasting Partnership of Ideas

While Einstein initially viewed Minkowski's mathematical reformulation with some reservation, considering it superfluous, he eventually embraced this geometric perspective. The Minkowski spacetime concept proved essential when Einstein later developed his general theory of relativity in 1915, which described gravity as the curvature of spacetime itself.

## Conclusion

Starting from Einstein's physical insights and enriched by Minkowski's mathematical genius, the theory of relativity reshaped our understanding of reality. Together, their contributions form the foundation upon which much of modern physics still rests today.
